summary: What prototypes are, the advantages and disadvantages of prototyping, and how to design prototypes of interfaces, input forms and output forms.

blocks.content: An **early, simplified working model** of a system (or part of it, usually the interface) that is shown to users to get **feedback** before the full system is built.

items.title: Throw-away prototype
items.content: Built quickly (even on paper or in a design tool), used to collect feedback, then **discarded**; the real system is built from scratch.

items.title: Evolutionary prototype
items.content: Improved step by step after each round of feedback until it **becomes the final system**.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages of prototyping
rows: Users see and try the system early, so **misunderstandings are found early**
Users may think the prototype is the finished system and expect it soon
Requirements can be refined from feedback
Repeated changes can increase **time and cost**
Users feel involved → more likely to accept the system
Focus on the interface may hide problems with the processing/data
Errors are cheaper to fix at the design stage
Helps the developer estimate the work needed
Scope may grow ("can it also do …?")

theory.title: Designing interface, input and output prototypes

items.title: Interface design
items.content: Layout of screens and navigation: menus, buttons, consistent colours and fonts, clear headings, help messages.

items.title: Input form design
items.content: Fields in a logical order, clear **labels**, suitable controls (drop-down lists, radio buttons, check boxes, date pickers), **validation** and error messages, default values.

items.title: Output form design
items.content: Reports and screens that show results clearly: headings, tables, totals, charts; only the information the user needs; printable.
